primitives.name: Variance-Aware Z-Score
primitives.verbatim_quote: Method / model - Z-score (baseline): z = (μ(q) - μ) / σ, where σ is the cross-player standard deviation.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'μ(q)': "player's weekly mean performance (dimensionless)", 'μ': 'population mean performance (dimensionless)', 'σ': 'cross-player standard deviation (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Player performance follows static distribution; no form or injury dynamics.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When player variance dominates cross-player variance, Z-score becomes unstable.

layer2.mapping: G-score extends Z-score by adding player-specific variance to the denominator, making valuation robust to individual volatility.

primitives.name: G-Score
primitives.verbatim_quote: - G-score: adds the player's own period-to-period variance τ2, scaled by κ, to the denominator.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'μ(q)': "player's weekly mean performance (dimensionless)", 'μ': 'population mean performance (dimensionless)', 'σ': 'cross-player standard deviation (dimensionless)', 'τ': "player's week-to-week standard deviation (dimensionless)", 'κ': 'scaling factor for player variance (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Static distributions, random teammate assignment, equal game weight.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When κ → 0, G-score reduces to Z-score; when κ → ∞, variance dominates.

The G-score is derived from the standard Z-score by incorporating a player’s own variance into the denominator. This adjustment reflects that high-variance players may offer less reliable value than low-variance ones, even if their average performance is similar. The formula introduces a scaling parameter κ which quantifies how much a player's internal variability should be considered relative to population-level variability. In simulations, this leads to higher win rates for G-score-based drafting strategies compared to traditional Z-score methods. The key insight is that variance-aware valuation improves decision-making under uncertainty, particularly in head-to-head formats where consistency matters. The failure mode occurs when assumptions break down—such as non-static distributions or positional scarcity—which can lead to overfitting or misapplication of the model.
